title: Almont Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Almont wells have a 95 ft median depth, with finished well costs commonly modeled at $12,200-$21,500.
h1: What Almont Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Almont sits in mountain terrain where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Records within 5 miles show 487 permitted wells, giving a useful local picture of depth, yield, water levels, drilling history, and likely construction cost.

The numbers are not a guarantee for a particular lot. Fractured granite and gneiss can change quickly across short distances. Before buying land or bidding a new well, review nearby well permits, confirm the intended household use with Colorado DWR, and have a driller evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, and pump requirements.

sections.heading: Almont well depth is usually modest, but bedrock controls the result
sections.html:
Almont wells have a median reported depth of 95 feet. The middle half runs from 57 to 180 feet, so a typical drilling bid may be based on a relatively shallow hole, but the spread is substantial. Fifty-two percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 33% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Depth becomes less predictable in fractured mountain rock. Fifteen percent of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 850 feet. Those deeper examples matter when comparing properties: a nearby successful well does not prove that the same fracture will continue beneath a new homesite.

sections.heading: Yields around Almont are generally strong on the reported wells
sections.html:
Among the 124 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-seven percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 27% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Six percent produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are reported below 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for a buyer, but it is not a promise for an unbuilt lot. Ask what the permitted use allows and have the completed well tested. Household demand also depends on storage, pump capacity, fixtures, and any livestock or irrigation plans.

sections.heading: Water levels show no simple evidence of a dropping table
sections.html:
The median static water level is 40 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 30 and 100 feet. Only 42 records report a static water level, so this is a smaller sample than the depth records and should be treated as a local reference rather than a site-specific measurement.

By measurement decade, the median was 44 feet below surface in the 2010s and 35 feet in the 2020s. That series does not show a deeper median water level in the newer decade. Water levels can still vary by season, elevation, recharge, and fracture connection, so a driller or hydrologist should evaluate the actual parcel.

sections.heading: Almont’s permit history points to long local drilling experience
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records include permits from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. The largest group is from the 1990s, with 130 permits. Records also show 70 permits from the 2000s, 60 from the 2010s, and 23 from the 2020s.

Bob Williams Drilling Co., listed as Williams, Robert F., appears most often with 222 records. Sharpe Drilling Co. has 17, and Mark A. Huffington has 13. These records show who has worked in the area; they are not a quality ranking. Confirm current licensing, availability, references, access requirements, and the written scope before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Almont well models at $12,200 to $21,500 finished
sections.html:
The local cost model uses fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at $65 to $100 per foot. At the 95-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $6,200 to $9,500.

A finished well adds the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work. The modeled total is about $12,200 to $21,500 at the median depth. A deeper hole can move beyond that range, and difficult access, casing, grout, rock conditions, water testing, power distance, and site preparation may add cost. Request an itemized bid that separates drilling from completion and allowances.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic layout, access, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 27 historic mine features, and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These facts do not establish a problem on a particular parcel. They do support checking environmental records, historic land use, mine features, and laboratory water testing before closing or occupying a home.

Most permits are for domestic or household use at 80%; stock use is 8%, irrigation is 3%, and monitoring is 6%. Confirm the permit’s allowed use before planning gardens, animals, or additional buildings. Locate the well and septic system together, preserve required separation, plan equipment access, and confirm power and driveway grades. A dry hole or low-yield result remains possible in fractured bedrock even where nearby wells perform well.

sections.heading: What to do before buying an Almont lot
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit map and compare the closest completed wells, not just the countywide averages. Look for reported depth, yield, static water level, construction details, and the named aquifer. Around Almont, 481 permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer conditions, while 3 identify alluvial water and 1 identifies the Mesa Verde Group. No recorded wells identify the Denver Basin aquifer.

For a buildable parcel, obtain a driller’s access and cost review before removing inspection contingencies. Ask about a drilling depth allowance, casing and grout, pump testing, storage, electrical service, trenching, septic suitability, and water-quality testing. If the property is near Crested Butte, Gunnison, Mount Crested Butte, Pitkin, Garfield, or Marble, do not assume conditions match Almont; compare the actual nearby permits and geology.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Almont, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Almont is 95 feet. The middle half runs from 57 to 180 feet, but 15% are between 300 and 600 feet and the deepest record is 850 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make depth variable, so nearby permits help but cannot guarantee a new well depth.

faq.q: How much water do Almont wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half falls between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-seven percent of reporting wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures come from 124 yield records, so a buyer should still require a completed-well test and confirm the permitted household or other use.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Almont?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 95-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $6,200 to $9,500. Including a pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished well models at $12,200 to $21,500. Access, deeper drilling, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Almont?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 1 PFAS sampling or contamination site, 27 historic mine features, and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test water from the specific well for relevant contaminants, review nearby land and mine history, and retest after construction or any change in water quality.

faq.q: Do Almont wells have enough water for a home?
faq.a: Reported yields are generally favorable: the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, 67% of reporting wells exceed 15 gallons per minute, and 0% report below 1 gallon per minute. Still, only 124 wells report yield, and household adequacy depends on storage, pump performance, permitted use, and the home’s demand. Verify the actual well before relying on it.
